 Julius Randle calls for Nets to get on the same page defensively

 Nets’ Julius Randle called out his team’s defense this season. 
 By C.J. Holmes | cholmes@nydailynews.com | New York Daily News PUBLISHED: October 27, 2026 at 3:22 PM EDT With 2:45 left before halftime Sunday, Mo Wagner’s 3-pointer gave the Nets a 51-49 lead over Indiana Pacers . By the break, Brooklyn trailed by nine.
 The Pacers’ 16-5 run was a costly example of the lapses Julius Randle wants Brooklyn to recognize before a game gets out of control. After a 136-109 loss, the veteran forward identified a problem that reaches beyond any one bad stretch: the Nets aren’t consistently working together on defense.
 That’s painfully obvious three games into the season.
 “We’re just not all on the same page. Got to find a way to communicate better, respect communication amongst each other,” Randle said. “If a guy calls something, we have to honor the call.”
 Brooklyn’s frequent switching makes those calls essential. Trading assignments require defenders to agree on the exchange and teammates around them to adjust. A call only helps if somebody acts on it.
 Michael Porter Jr. described another challenge in Brooklyn’s coverages. Bringing a defender up to the level of a ball screen creates pressure on the ball handler. But a pass to the screener rolling toward the basket can leave teammates behind the play outnumbered.
 “We want to get deflections and speed teams up, but we’re at a disadvantage,” Porter said. “So, we have to be really on our horse to scramble and get to shooters and close out and try to take guys off the 3-point line. Because a lot of times we are playing four-on-three, and we’ve gotta get out of that situation and scramble a little bit better.”
 The defender who moves to stop the ball needs someone else to cover the space left behind. Each rotation buys a teammate time to recover, provided the next player moves with it.
 The Nets collected seven steals in the opening quarter, then allowed 112 points over the remaining three. Head coach Jordi Fernández called the performance after the first quarter “unacceptable” and said he needed to help his players more.
 Even getting organized after a basket proved difficult. Indiana scored 25 fast-break points, and Nolan Traoré said the Pacers were running before Brooklyn could get set.
 “Even on made basket, they were always running and we couldn’t get back,” Traoré said.
 That leaves the Nets scrambling before they can establish their coverage. Communication has to start while players are finding opponents in transition, then continue as they navigate screens and help each other.
 Randle wants that awareness to extend to the rhythm of a game. An opponent stringing together baskets or Brooklyn committing consecutive turnovers should be a warning to the group, he said.
 Ahead of Tuesday’s game in Boston, Brooklyn listed Joshua Jefferson, Drake Powell and Ben Saraf as out on G League assignment. Tyler Bilodeau and Grant Nelson were also listed out under G League two-way designations.
 Randle put the burden on the players to make the system work. When asked whether the Nets were still learning Fernández’s scheme, the forward made clear that understanding the instructions wasn’t the issue.
 “No, I think we understand what we need to do,” Randle said. “I think we just got to execute it better. Us as players, we got to execute it better.”
